passage: The school hall in Nagpur buzzed as Principal Mr. Deshmukh announced the drawing prize. Irawati's name was read out, and she skipped to the stage. Sarika sat in the third row with her hands clenched in her lap. She had worked on her own peacock for two weeks. Her stomach twisted. Then she pressed her lips together, stood up and clapped hard, and when Irawati came back down she said, “Well done, it's beautiful.” Irawati beamed. At lunch, Sarika sat quietly. She whispered to a friend, “I wanted it too. But I am happy for her.” Her friend squeezed her hand.

qa.q: How long had Sarika worked on her peacock?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as she clapped for Irawati, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was disappointed and a little envious, since her hands were clenched and her stomach twisted, yet she chose to celebrate.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that helped her handle the mixed feelings?
qa.a: She congratulated Irawati and then named her feeling privately to a friend, so she did not pretend it was not there.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt hearing Sarika's congratulation?
qa.a: She probably felt warm and pleased, since she beamed, and she may not have guessed Sarika was also disappointed.

grounding: A child claps and congratulates a winner while feeling disappointed, and privately names the feeling to a friend.

passage: At the district swimming gala in Pune, I sat behind Naveen and Suraj on the bleachers. Suraj had come second, and Naveen had won the race. When the results were called, Suraj sat very still and stared at his hands. Then he stood up and hugged Naveen, saying, “Great swim!” It looked a bit stiff. Later I overheard him tell his father, “I really wanted to win.” His father said, “That's fair. You can feel both.” Suraj nodded and drank his juice. I couldn't tell how long the disappointment would last, but he seemed honest about it.

qa.q: Who won the swimming race?
qa.a: Naveen.

qa.q: What did Suraj's stiff hug and quiet stare suggest about how he felt, and what else might explain them?
qa.a: They suggest he was disappointed but trying to be a good sport, though he might also have been simply tired after the race.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father do that helped?
qa.a: He said it is fair to want to win and that his son could feel both, so the feeling was named and not hidden.

qa.q: How might Naveen have seen Suraj's hug?
qa.a: Naveen may have taken it as real congratulation, or perhaps noticed the stiffness, so he could not be sure how Suraj felt.

grounding: A child congratulates the winner while disappointed, seen by an observer, and later names the feeling to a parent.

passage: Sunday diary. Today Nani came from Jaipur and I did what I always do: I bent down, touched her feet and said “Namaste, Nani.” She put her hand on my head and smiled. Then I went to the balcony and greeted Mr. Khan next door with “Assalamu alaikum, uncle.” He waved and said, “Good boy.” My friend Francis came for cricket and I told him about it. He said in his family they say “Good morning, Grandma” and kiss her cheek. We laughed. I think everyone shows respect in their own way. I like how the greeting makes people smile. Samir.

qa.q: Where did Nani come from?
qa.a: Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he greeted Nani and Mr. Khan?
qa.a: Samir was comfortable and pleased, since he did what he always does and noticed how the greeting made people smile.

qa.q: What did Francis's story add to the conversation?
qa.a: It showed that in his family greetings for elders are different, a spoken good morning and a kiss on the cheek.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Samir touched her feet?
qa.a: Nani smiled and put a hand on his head, so she probably felt loved and respected.

grounding: A child greets elders with a touch on the feet and respectful address, and learns that the form varies by family.

passage: In the lane of a small town near Nashik, Lokesh saw Shankar's grandfather coming home from the temple with his walking stick. Lokesh stopped kicking the ball, folded his hands and said, “Namaste, Dada-ji.” Shankar, a step behind, bent and touched the old man's feet. Dada-ji patted each head and asked, “Have you both eaten?” They nodded. Dada-ji chuckled. “Then go and play.” Lokesh grinned. At his own home the family did not touch feet, but folded hands and said “ji” to elders. Shankar whispered, “Different ways, same respect.” They went back to the ball, smiling.

qa.q: What did Dada-ji carry?
qa.a: A walking stick.

qa.q: What did Lokesh and Shankar seem to feel towards Dada-ji, and what shows it?
qa.a: They felt respect and warmth, shown by stopping their game, greeting him and answering his question.

qa.q: What does the difference between the two children's greetings show?
qa.a: It shows that the form of respect varies by family, since Lokesh folded his hands and Shankar touched feet.

qa.q: How might Dada-ji have felt when the children stopped their game to greet him?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and cared for, since he patted each head and chuckled.

grounding: A child greets an elder with namaste and touches feet, showing respect and belonging, and the form differs by family.

passage:
Monday. In art class, Akash noticed Aparna's drawing of a lighthouse and said quietly, “That's really good.” Aparna went pink and said nothing.

Wednesday. Aparna scored a goal at break. Akash clapped. “Great shot!” She smiled and said, “Thanks for saying so on Monday, too.”

Friday. Akash's pencil box fell and everything rolled away. Aparna helped him pick up the pieces. “Thank you,” he said. Later, Ms. Rana wondered whether the compliments were just friendly or a way of gaining a partner for the class project. Akash said, “No, I just liked them.” Aparna believed him.

qa.q: On which day did Aparna score a goal?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: Why might Aparna have gone pink and said nothing at Akash's first compliment?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and shy, since she had not expected it, though she remembered it later with thanks.

qa.q: What made Akash's compliments feel sincere to Aparna?
qa.a: He said them with no strings, repeated them over different days and thanked her when she helped, so his words matched his actions.

qa.q: Why might Ms. Rana wonder about the compliments?
qa.a: Compliments can be sincere or a way to gain favour, so context and reciprocity shape how they are heard, and she could not know Akash's reason from outside.

grounding: A child compliments a classmate's drawing and goal and thanks for help, and context shapes how compliments are heard.

passage: Jatin, you asked why I say thank you so often. Let me tell you about a boy in my class named Amandeep when I was twelve. One day Amandeep said to me, “That's a great answer!” after I spoke in class. I felt warm all day. Some weeks later, Amandeep asked to copy my homework and started saying nice things every day. I began to wonder: was it real? I asked myself whether he would say it if he had nothing to gain. Some were real, some were not. I learned to thank sincerely, and to notice whether compliments came with strings. Say thanks, but think, too.

qa.q: How old was the storyteller when Amandeep gave the compliment?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller begin to doubt Amandeep's compliments?
qa.a: The storyteller wondered whether the compliments were real or a way to get something, since they came with a request.

qa.q: What can a child learn from this story about thanking and complimenting?
qa.a: To thank sincerely and to notice whether a compliment comes with strings.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt if he was truly friendly and was doubted?
qa.a: He might feel hurt if his kind words were seen as tricks, which shows why context and reciprocity matter.

grounding: An elder shows that compliments can be sincere or a way to gain favour, so context and reciprocity shape how they are heard.

passage: In a Tokyo classroom, Olga's paper boat fell in the puddle, and she cried. Yuki felt a squeeze in her own chest, as if she were the one who had lost the boat. She also felt sorry, thinking, “Poor Olga.” Then she stopped herself. “Maybe she's angry, not sad,” she thought. She said, “Do you want company?” Olga sniffed and nodded. Yuki sat on the step beside her and said nothing else. After a few minutes Olga said, “I worked so hard on that.” Yuki nodded. “It looked great. Should we make another one together?” Olga wiped her eyes and smiled a little.

qa.q: What fell in the puddle?
qa.a: Olga's paper boat.

qa.q: What did Yuki feel when Olga cried, and what was the difference between the two feelings?
qa.a: Yuki felt with Olga, a squeeze in her own chest, and also felt sorry for her, and then remembered she might be wrong about the emotion.

qa.q: Why was asking Do you want company a wise choice?
qa.a: Yuki could have guessed wrongly that Olga was sad, so asking let Olga say what she wanted.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt about Yuki's company?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and understood, since she nodded and then shared that she had worked hard.

grounding: A child feels with another and feels sorry for her, and asks Do you want company because guessing can be wrong.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5, Vishal and Usha. During art class, Usha's water bottle spilled over her drawing, and she went quiet. Vishal noticed and, before I could speak, he walked over. He looked at the drawing and said, “That's a lot of work gone.” His face looked sad, too. Then he added, “Do you want me to stay, or do you want to be alone?” Usha said, “Stay.” He sat with her and helped blot the paper. I want to praise how he asked and did not assume. Sometimes he guesses feelings from the situation, so he is learning that asking is wiser. Mr. Gupta.

qa.q: What spilled over Usha's drawing?
qa.a: Her water bottle.

qa.q: What was Vishal probably feeling as he looked at the ruined drawing?
qa.a: He seemed to feel sad along with Usha, and also sorry for her, since his face looked sad and he offered to stay.

qa.q: What did the teacher praise about how Vishal handled it?
qa.a: He asked whether Usha wanted him to stay or be alone, instead of assuming what she felt.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Vishal asked her a choice?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and comforted, since she chose to have him stay.

grounding: A child feels with another and learns the difference from feeling sorry, guessing from the situation but asking is wiser.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: The storm knocked out the lights on the morning of the district race, and the school hall in Kanpur echoed with wind. Zeenat sat on the wet steps with her shoes untied, her hands shaking. Her friend Dilnaz crouched next to her. “I'm scared,” said Zeenat. “I know,” said Dilnaz. “You're nervous. That's okay. But you can do it. Try to run the first bend slowly and speed up when you see the flag.” Zeenat took a breath. “Okay.” Dilnaz tied her shoe. “You can do it,” she said again. Zeenat stood up, and they walked out together to the track.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz tie?
qa.a: Zeenat's shoe.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on the steps, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt scared and nervous about the race, shown by her shaking hands and her saying “I'm scared.”

qa.q: What made Dilnaz's encouragement helpful?
qa.a: She did not deny the nervousness, said it was okay, and gave a concrete suggestion about running the first bend slowly.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel about her friend's race?
qa.a: She probably cares and wants to give belief and help, and she may also feel a little nervous herself. 🙂

grounding: A child says you can do it before a race, acknowledges nervousness and gives a concrete suggestion.

subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
passage: “You can do it, Jahnavi!” said Akash, tapping her desk before the spelling test. “I can't,” she said, her fingers cold. “What if I forget?” Akash didn't tell her to stop worrying. He said, “Everybody gets nervous. Look at the words once, then read them slowly as you write.” Jahnavi nodded and took a long breath. “Okay. Slowly.” He gave her a small thumbs-up and went to his seat. During the test she wrote each word as slowly as she could. Later she told Akash, “I was still nervous, but the slow part helped.” He grinned.

qa.q: What test was Jahnavi about to take?
qa.a: A spelling test.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say she couldn't do it?
qa.a: She was nervous and worried she would forget the words, which is why her fingers were cold.

qa.q: What made Akash's encouragement more than a slogan?
qa.a: He said everyone gets nervous and gave a concrete tip to look at the words once and read slowly.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Jahnavi thanked him?
qa.a: He was probably happy that his help mattered, since he grinned.

grounding: A child says you can do it before a test, does not deny nervousness and gives a concrete suggestion.

passage: The clay pot fell out of Sharmila's hands as she rushed across the classroom in the crowded corridor, and it cracked on the floor. It was Minakshi's pot, made for the school display and due to be shown in ten minutes. Sharmila's heart thumped. She wanted to say “It just slipped” but she did not. “I broke it,” she said. “I'm sorry. I was running.” Minakshi's eyes filled. Sharmila added, “I can help you fix it with glue, or make another with you at lunch.” Minakshi took a breath. “Let's glue it first.” They found the teacher, and together they mended the pot.

qa.q: Whose pot broke?
qa.a: Minakshi's.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she said “I broke it”?
qa.a: She felt guilty and worried, since her heart thumped, and she chose to own up instead of making an excuse.

qa.q: What made Sharmila's apology repair more than a vague sorry?
qa.a: She named exactly what she did, said she was running and offered to fix or remake the pot.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt at first, and what changed?
qa.a: She was upset and near tears at first, then more settled when Sharmila offered specific help. 🤍

grounding: A child says I broke it, I'm sorry, and offers to help fix it, naming the act and offering a remedy.

passage: “I broke your torch, Jagdish,” said Afreen at the door, holding the two pieces. “I was using it under the bed and it fell. I'm really sorry.” Jagdish looked at it, then at her. “It was my birthday present.” Afreen swallowed. “I know. I'll give you my pocket money for a new one, or we can take it to the repair shop together this weekend. Which do you want?” Jagdish sighed. “Repair shop, I think.” Afreen's shoulders dropped. She said, “Thank you for letting me help.” Jagdish put a hand on the pieces. “Thanks for telling me the truth.”

qa.q: What did Afreen break?
qa.a: Jagdish's torch.

qa.q: What was Jagdish probably feeling when saying it was a birthday present?
qa.a: Jagdish was probably hurt and sad about losing something special, though also willing to accept help.

qa.q: Why is Afreen's apology more repairing than a vague sorry?
qa.a: She named what she did, said she was sorry and offered a real remedy with a choice.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt while she waited for Jagdish's answer?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and guilty, and relieved when Jagdish chose the repair shop.

grounding: A child says I broke it, I'm sorry, and offers to replace or fix it, naming the act and the remedy.

passage:
Monday. Bhavna and Kunal had a quarrel at recess over who had to give up the swing. Bhavna said, “You're mean,” and Kunal walked off. They did not speak.

Wednesday. Bhavna felt lonely at lunch. Kunal came over slowly and said, “Sorry about the swing.” Bhavna said, “It's okay, let's play.” Kunal grinned, but Bhavna's smile was small.

Friday. At the swing, Kunal started grabbing again. Bhavna said, “I forgave you, but I don't want to be pushed. Let's take turns properly.” Kunal thought. “Okay. You first.”

qa.q: On which day did Kunal apologise about the swing?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Bhavna probably feeling when saying “It's okay, let's play” with a small smile?
qa.a: Bhavna likely felt lonely and wanted to be friends again, though the small smile suggests Bhavna still felt a little hurt.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do on Friday that showed forgiveness does not mean accepting the behaviour again?
qa.a: Bhavna said “I forgave you” but did not want to be pushed, and asked for proper turns.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Bhavna spoke up on Friday?
qa.a: Kunal was probably surprised, then thoughtful, since Kunal agreed to let Bhavna go first.

grounding: A child forgives a friend after a quarrel with it's okay, let's play, but the hurtful behaviour need not be accepted again.

passage: Bhavna, my dear, you asked why I told you not to say “It's okay” when it is not. Let me tell you about my friend Minakshi. When we were eleven, she tore my favourite book and said sorry. I said, “It's okay, let's play,” because I was afraid to lose her. But it was not okay, and my stomach ached all day. The next week she tore another. Then I told her, “I forgive you, but it was hurtful, and I need you to be careful.” She was quiet, then said, “I didn't know it mattered.” We stayed friends, and she was careful afterwards.

qa.q: How old were the two friends when Minakshi tore the book?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller say “It's okay” when it was not?
qa.a: The storyteller was afraid to lose Minakshi as a friend, so said it to avoid conflict.

qa.q: What did the storyteller learn to say instead?
qa.a: “I forgive you, but it was hurtful, and I need you to be careful.”

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when she learned it mattered?
qa.a: She said she did not know it mattered, so she probably felt surprised and sorry, and willing to be more careful.

grounding: Forgiveness can be real or a way to avoid conflict, and it does not mean the hurtful behaviour should be accepted again.

passage: The nurse's room at the school in Lagos had a chart with little faces from smiling to crying. Ada sat on the bed holding her stomach. “Where does it hurt?” asked the nurse. Ada pointed to the left side. “What kind of pain?” “Like a twist.” “How strong? Point to a face.” Ada pointed to the middle face. Yosef, her cousin, said, “She said it was nothing at breakfast.” Ada looked at her shoes. “I didn't want a fuss.” The nurse nodded. “I'm glad you told me now. I'll call your aunt so a doctor can look if it keeps going.”

qa.q: Where did Ada point to when the nurse asked where it hurt?
qa.a: To the left side of her stomach.

qa.q: Why did Ada say nothing at breakfast, and how do you know?
qa.a: She did not want a fuss, which she admitted by looking at her shoes and saying so.

qa.q: What did the nurse do that helped Ada describe the pain?
qa.a: The nurse asked for the place, the kind and how strong, using a chart of faces.

qa.q: How might Yosef have felt about telling the nurse what Ada said?
qa.a: Yosef probably felt worried about Ada and wanted her to get help. 🙂

grounding: A child describes pain by place, kind and level using a chart, and some children downplay pain to avoid fuss.

passage: In the clinic waiting room at the community centre, Francis waited with his mother while a volunteer, Ankita, handed out colouring sheets. When the nurse called his name, he winced as he stood. “Show me on the picture of a body where it hurts,” said the nurse. Francis coloured a spot on his ankle red. “Is it sharp or dull?” “Sharp, like a pinch.” “How big? Small, medium or big?” “Medium.” He had been limping for days and telling everyone he was fine. His mother said quietly, “You told me you were fine.” Francis stared at the floor. “I didn't want to miss football.”

qa.q: Where did Francis colour the spot on the body picture?
qa.a: On his ankle.

qa.q: Why did Francis tell everyone he was fine?
qa.a: He did not want to miss football, so he downplayed the pain.

qa.q: What could Francis's mother and the nurse do next?
qa.a: They could listen to how the ankle feels, and check with the doctor since he had been limping and the pain kept going.

qa.q: How might Ankita, the volunteer, see the scene?
qa.a: Ankita may see a boy who is hurting and worried, and can help by offering a calm, friendly space while he waits.

grounding: A child describes pain by place, kind and size, and downplays it to avoid missing football, so changed behaviour deserves attention.

passage: In a shop in Hanoi, Daniel held two rain jackets, a yellow one and a green one. “I like the yellow one better,” he said to his friend Tuan. “The green one is too plain.” His father shook his head. “The yellow is smaller, Daniel. It won't fit next winter.” Daniel frowned. “But I don't want the green one. It looks like school.” Tuan said, “What about the yellow, if it can be let out at the sleeves?” Daniel's father smiled. “Good idea. Let's ask the shopkeeper.” Daniel nodded, relieved that they had listened. He still wanted yellow, but he understood his father's reason.

qa.q: What colours were the two jackets?
qa.a: Yellow and green.

qa.q: Why did Daniel say he did not want the green one?
qa.a: He thought it looked like school and too plain, so he preferred the yellow.

qa.q: What helped the family find a solution?
qa.a: Tuan's idea about letting out the sleeves, and Daniel's father listening and giving a reason.

qa.q: How might Daniel's father see Daniel's preference?
qa.a: He probably takes it as valid, and his reason about fit shows he wants a jacket that lasts.

grounding: A child states a preference and gives reasons, and explaining limits respectfully keeps trust.

passage: After lunch in the school garden, Zubin's group had to choose between painting the fence or planting seeds. “I don't want to paint,” said Zubin. “It's boring.” The teacher, Afreen, asked, “Why do you prefer seeds?” Zubin thought. “I like watching things grow, and painting is just waiting.” Afreen said, “That's a clear reason. We can't all plant today because we only have six pots. Could you plant first, and paint next week?” Zubin frowned, then nodded. “Okay, if I go first.” Afreen smiled. “Deal.” Zubin bounced over to the pots, still a little disappointed but pleased to be heard.

qa.q: How many pots did the group have?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Zubin prefer planting seeds?
qa.a: Zubin liked watching things grow and found painting boring, like waiting.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that helped Zubin accept part of what Zubin did not want?
qa.a: Afreen asked for Zubin's reason, praised it and offered a fair deal, planting first and painting next week.

qa.q: How might other children in the group feel about Zubin going first?
qa.a: Some might feel it is unfair, so the teacher may want to explain the turn-taking so everyone feels heard.

grounding: A child says I don't want to paint, gives reasons, and negotiates while the adult explains limits respectfully.

passage: Counsellor's note. Jahnavi came to me at break, upset, saying that Rafiq had cheated in the relay by starting early. “It's not fair,” she said. I asked what she had seen, and she described it carefully. I told her I would check with the sports teacher. She wanted to tell the whole class, which I discouraged, but I said her concern for fairness was real. I suggested she say what she saw and leave the decision to the teacher. She nodded, still frowning. Later Rafiq said he'd misheard the starter. I will talk with both about tone next week. Ms. Kaur.

qa.q: Who did Jahnavi say had cheated in the relay?
qa.a: Rafiq.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she reported Rafiq?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and was upset, which shows a genuine concern for fairness.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest, and why?
qa.a: She suggested Jahnavi say what she saw and leave the decision to the teacher, so the concern is heard without turning into tale-telling.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when he learns he was reported?
qa.a: He may feel accused and defensive, since he says he misheard the starter, so tone and care matter.

grounding: A child criticises a teammate as unfair and reports rule breaking, and an adult guides tone.

passage: Thursday. Today in PE Vandana kept giving herself extra turns at the rope. I told her twice that it wasn't fair. She said I was bossy. I felt hot. I'm not trying to be bossy, I just hate it when the rules are bent. Payal said I should go to Sir, but I think I sounded like a tattletale when I did. Sir said thank you for telling him and would handle it. Later, Mummy said it's good to care about fairness, but to say it kindly first. Tomorrow I will say “Can we count turns?” before I run to Sir.

qa.q: How many times did the writer tell Vandana it wasn't fair?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did the writer feel hot when Vandana said bossy?
qa.a: The writer felt misunderstood, since the concern was about fairness and not about being in charge.

qa.q: What could the writer try tomorrow?
qa.a: Say something kind first, like “Can we count turns?” before going to Sir.

qa.q: How might Vandana see the writer's complaint?
qa.a: Vandana may feel accused and see it as bossy, which shows why tone matters.

grounding: A child criticises unfair turns and reports rule breaking, and learns tone matters to avoid sounding bossy.
